events.title: The Dinner Table
events.body: The rectory at {parish} eats at six. You learn this the way you learn most things in your first week, by getting it wrong: you come down at half past with your breviary under your arm and find {@pastor} halfway through a plate of something the cook left under foil, the television on with the sound off, a glass of wine at his elbow and a second glass, empty, set at the place across from him. He does not comment. He asks about the funeral you took that afternoon, listens, tells you the family has been a problem since the grandfather sold the farm, and goes back to the news. It is not unfriendly. It is a man who has eaten alone at this table for eleven years and has not decided yet whether that is about to change. The cook has left a note on the counter about Fridays. The housekeeper has already moved your shoes. There is a rhythm to the house and you are the new element in it, and the question of the first month is whether you become part of the rhythm or a thing it works around.
events.flavorPrompt: The domestic texture of a rectory: foil, a muted television, a second glass set out and not explained.

choices.label: Come down at six every night and stay until he gets up
choices.outcome: By the third week he has started saving the paper for you. He talks more than you expected and less than you hoped, mostly about the parish's dead, whom he knows better than its living. You lose an hour most evenings you had meant for something else. You gain a man who, when he tells you a thing, tells it to you at that table first.

choices.label: Keep your own hours and eat when your day allows
choices.outcome: He never says a word about it. The second glass stops appearing after a fortnight. You have the evenings for the hospital, the breviary, the people who need you at seven. You also have a landlord rather than a pastor, and it will take a long time to find out which of you decided that.

choices.label: Ask the cook to put you both on the same plate and say nothing to him
choices.outcome: The cook looks at you as if you have proposed something unusual, which you have. From Thursday there is one dish, hot, and two plates, and he comes down to find the table set for two without either of you having arranged it. He grunts. The housekeeper, who sees everything, tells the secretary you are a sly one, which is the nicest thing she will say about you for a year.

events.title: The Six O'Clock
events.body: The weekday schedule at {parish} has a 6:30 Mass that {@pastor} has said every morning for a decade, and a 8:30 that draws the retired, the school parents, and whoever the 6:30 was too early for. In your second month he hands you a sheet. You have the 6:30. All of them. He has moved himself to the 8:30 permanently, because, he says, his knees, and because it is good for a young priest to see who comes to church in the dark: the nurses coming off shift, the man who opens the hardware store, the widow who has not slept since March. He is not wrong about that. He is also not asking. The sheet has no end date. The daily Mass crowd at 6:30 is about fourteen people, and they will notice within a week that the pastor has stopped coming, and they will decide what that means about you. Your day off is on the sheet too, and it is Monday, which is the day you had not wanted.
events.flavorPrompt: A schedule handed over as a fact. The dark morning crowd described with respect.

choices.label: Take the 6:30, and take it seriously
choices.outcome: You are up at five for the rest of your time here. By Advent you know all fourteen by name and the nurses have started staying for the rosary because you stay. It is the most reliable thing about you and it costs you every late night you might have wanted. {@pastor} takes it as settled and forgets, you suspect, that he ever arranged it.

choices.label: Propose alternating weeks, and put it in writing
choices.outcome: You type it up: odd weeks yours, even weeks his, day off rotating. He reads it standing up. He says he will think about it, which means no, and then two weeks later says fine, which means he told someone at the deanery and they laughed at him. The 6:30 gets both of you and grumbles about it. You have won something small and he remembers.

choices.label: Take the Mass, but ask for a different day off
choices.outcome: He is so relieved about the 6:30 that he gives you Thursday without a fight. You have learned something about how he negotiates: everything is a trade, and he does not keep score of the trades he wins. The 6:30 becomes yours. Thursday becomes the day the secretary cannot find you, which she minds more than he does.

events.title: The Keys
events.body: You ask {@secretary} for a key to the sacramental registers cabinet and are told, pleasantly, that Father keeps that key. You ask {@pastor} and he says she has it. This is the first time you notice that the parish office at {parish} has an org chart nobody drew. The secretary answers the phone, and so decides which calls reach a priest and which are handled. She keeps the Mass intention book, and so decides which families get the Sunday slot in May. She types the bulletin, keeps the calendar, and knows the assessment figure before the pastor does. She has been here nineteen years, through three pastors, and she is not unkind and not dishonest. She is simply the continuity, and the priests are the weather. You have been assigned a desk in the room off hers. From it you can hear her tell a caller that Father is unavailable when you are sitting six feet away, doing nothing, available.
events.flavorPrompt: The undrawn org chart. The secretary is competent and long-serving, not a villain.

choices.label: Learn her system and ask to be given a place in it
choices.outcome: You sit with her for an afternoon and let her explain the intention book, the funeral home contacts, which families are not to be put through to the pastor before ten. It is a better briefing than the chancery gave you. From then on she screens for you as carefully as she screens for him, and you are inside the machine, which is where the calls are.

choices.label: Get your own line, your own key, and your own calendar
choices.outcome: It takes a month and one conversation with {@pastor} that he plainly does not enjoy. You get the key. The secretary's manner toward you becomes exact. Calls for you reach you. Calls for a priest, when you are the only one in, somehow still wait for Father. You have your independence and the price of it, which is that the machine now works around you.

choices.label: Write her a job description and give it to the pastor to sign
choices.outcome: It is two pages and it is fair. It names what she does, which nobody has ever done, and it names what she does not decide, which is the point. {@pastor} signs it without reading and she reads it twice. She is, you are surprised to find, grateful for the first page and furious about the second, and the two feelings do not cancel. The office runs better and colder.

events.title: The Shower
events.body: The shower in the vicar's bathroom at {parish} produces hot water for ninety seconds and then something between a threat and a memory. You mention it to {@maintenance} in your second week and he nods as if you have told him the date. The predecessor mentioned it too. And the one before. The problem, he says, is the mixing valve and the problem behind the problem is the pipe run from the boiler, and the problem behind that is that the rectory was plumbed in 1961 by a parishioner who did it for free, and you get what you pay for. He can put a new valve in for two hundred and it will help for a year. He can do it right for four thousand, which means opening the wall, and {@pastor} will not open a wall in a house he expects to leave. You have three options and a cold shower, and you are beginning to understand that the maintenance man holds, in his head, the true condition of every building the parish owns, and that nobody has ever asked him for the list.
events.flavorPrompt: Small, physical, domestic. The maintenance man's quiet expertise.

choices.label: The valve. Two hundred dollars, and live with it
choices.outcome: He puts it in on a Tuesday. The water runs hot for four minutes now, which feels like luxury. He tells you, packing up, that the boiler is next, and you say you have heard, and he says no, you have not. You make a note. The note is the beginning of a list you will keep for the rest of your time here.

choices.label: Take the cold showers and spend nothing
choices.outcome: You get used to it faster than you expected. {@maintenance} respects it and says so, in the way of a man who has taken cold showers on purpose. The housekeeper thinks you are strange. {@pastor}, who has hot water, never learns there was a question. It is a small mortification and it does not make you holy, but it does not cost the parish anything either.

choices.label: Look at the pipe run yourself and do the job with him on a Saturday
choices.outcome: You open the wall together. He is right about the run and wrong about the valve, and you are right about the valve and wrong about how long it will take. It takes the whole day and six hundred in parts, and the water is hot in the morning and the wall is closed by Sunday. He has not had help in that house in nine years. He will tell you now what the estimates should say.

events.title: The Cook
events.body: The rectory cook at {parish} comes four days a week, leaves dinner under foil, and has cooked for {@pastor} for so long that the menu is a record of his preferences, which run to roasts and a horror of garlic. She is paid from the parish account, a fact you notice on the budget sheet and file away. In your first month she asks, once, whether there is anything you do not eat. You say no. That was a mistake. There is a great deal she cooks that you do not eat, and there is a Friday fish that you would rather not describe, and every night you leave food on the plate she reads it and says nothing and the housekeeper reports it. She is not a bad cook. She is a cook for one man, and that man has habits, and you are a guest in the habits. On Sunday after the last Mass she brings in a pie for the two of you. It is the first thing she has made with you in mind, and she stands in the doorway to watch you eat it.
events.flavorPrompt: Food as the language of a household. No comedy at the cook's expense.

choices.label: Eat what is put in front of you and praise the pie
choices.outcome: You learn to eat the fish. The pie becomes a Sunday thing. By spring she has quietly moved the menu three degrees in your direction and {@pastor} has not noticed. It costs you nothing but the food you do not like, which is, you decide, one of the smaller things a priest is asked to accept.

choices.label: Tell her you will cook for yourself two nights a week
choices.outcome: She takes it worse than you meant it and better than the housekeeper predicted. Two nights a week the kitchen is yours and you make what your mother made, and one night {@pastor} comes down early and eats it, and asks for it again. The cook does not forgive you exactly, but she starts asking what you want on Fridays, which is a form of peace.

choices.label: Tell her honestly what you eat and ask for one dish a week from home
choices.outcome: It is an awkward conversation and it takes four minutes. She writes it down. The following Thursday there is a dish on the table that is nearly what you asked for, and she has made enough for the pastor too, and he eats it without a word and takes seconds. The housekeeper tells the secretary that you have opinions. You do.

events.title: The Housekeeper's Opinions
events.body: The housekeeper at {parish} has cleaned the rectory since before {@pastor} arrived and will, she has said, clean it after he leaves. She has views. The last vicar, she tells you while doing your room, was a lovely boy who could not keep a shirt pressed and had women in the parlor at all hours, by which she means the bereavement group met there on Wednesdays. The one before him was a saint, or was until he was moved, and she has her own idea why he was moved. The pastor is a good man who drinks a bit, and the secretary thinks she runs the place, and the music director, well. You are drying your hands and she is folding and it goes on for twenty minutes. None of it is malicious and half of it is probably true, and all of it will be repeated, and the thing she has not yet said is what she has decided about you. She will decide within the month. The parish will hear her verdict before it hears your first homily.
events.flavorPrompt: A monologue overheard while folding. The housekeeper is the parish's oral record, unreliable and indispensable.

choices.label: Listen, say nothing, and remember all of it
choices.outcome: You learn more about {parish} in twenty minutes than in the chancery's briefing. You also learn what she will say about you, by hearing what she says about the others, and you keep your shirts pressed and your parlor door open. Her verdict, delivered to the secretary in November, is that you are quiet and might do. It is not nothing.

choices.label: Tell her, kindly, that you would rather not hear about the priests
choices.outcome: She stops mid-fold and looks at you as though you had refused a plate. She does not talk about the priests to you again. She talks about you to everyone else, and the word is that the new one is stuck up, which fades by Lent but does not vanish. {@pastor}, told about it, says you did the right thing and that it will cost you, and both are true.

choices.label: Ask her, carefully, why she thinks the one before was moved
choices.outcome: She tells you a version, and you know enough about how a diocese moves men to hear the shape under her version. It was money, or it was a woman, or it was the bishop's temper, and she believes the last because it is the one that keeps him a saint. You file it. You will hear his name again, and you will know that nobody in this house knows the truth of it.

events.title: The Day Off
events.body: Your day off is on the schedule and it has been on the schedule for four months, and you have taken it, by your own count, three times. The rest have gone to a funeral that could not be moved, a hospital call, a wedding rehearsal the pastor forgot, and twice to nothing at all: you were in the rectory and the phone rang and you were the one who picked up. {@pastor} takes his. He takes it like a sacrament, leaving Monday at nine and coming back Tuesday at dawn, and where he goes he has never said. He said to you once, in the first week, that a priest who does not take his day off is a priest who will be in trouble by fifty, and he said it with the certainty of a man describing his own file. This Monday there is nothing on the calendar. The secretary has pointedly not put anything on it. Your sister has asked twice when she will see you. The car has a full tank. It is nine in the morning and you are standing in the kitchen with your keys in your hand, and the office phone is ringing through the wall.
events.flavorPrompt: Keys in hand, phone ringing through the wall. The habit of not resting, described without judgement.

choices.label: Let it ring. Go
choices.outcome: You drive with the phone off. Your sister feeds you and asks nothing about the parish and you sleep nine hours in a bed that is not yours. The call was a woman asking about a Mass card. The secretary handled it. On Tuesday you say the 6:30 like a man who has slept, and the fourteen notice, and the pastor notices, and neither says a word about it, which is their approval.

choices.label: Answer it. There will be other Mondays
choices.outcome: It was a woman about a Mass card, and then a man about his mother, and then it was noon. You do not go. You tell yourself the sister can wait and she can, and she does, and the third time you tell her she stops asking, which is a thing that happens gradually and then is done. {@pastor} watches you not leave and says nothing at all.

choices.label: Go, but spend it with {@brother_priest} at the diocesan golf day
choices.outcome: It is not rest, quite. It is eighteen holes with priests who talk about the bishop, the assignments board, and who is about to be made a pastor. You come back knowing three things you did not, and one of them is about your own parish. Your sister gets a phone call from the car. It is a day off in the sense the presbyterate means it.

events.title: The Column
events.body: {@pastor} is away for two weeks and the bulletin has a column on the inside cover with his name on it that has run every Sunday for eleven years. {@secretary} needs four hundred words by Wednesday noon and has made it clear that she will not run a blank. The column is the most-read thing the parish produces. It is read in the pews before Mass, in the car after, and by a small, attentive group who read it for what it does not say. The pastor's columns are about the weather, the dead, the school, and once a year the assessment. He has never used it to teach and he has told you, more than once, that a bulletin is not a pulpit. You have a page and a deadline and no instructions, and the question is whether you write the column he would have written, or the one you would, and whether anybody but the attentive few can tell the difference. The secretary, passing your door, says four hundred words, Father, and not one about the new Missal translation, because the last time that happened she took the calls.
events.flavorPrompt: The bulletin as the parish's most-read text. The attentive few who read for absences.

choices.label: Write his column: the weather, the sick, the school raffle
choices.outcome: It is pleasant and it is nothing and it takes you an hour. Three people tell you they liked it. The secretary runs it without a change, which is her highest praise. You have learned to write in the parish's voice, which is a skill, and you have said nothing, which is also a skill, and you are not sure yet which one you were practicing.

choices.label: Use the page to teach something about the liturgy
choices.outcome: Four hundred words on why the priest faces where he faces and what the silence after Communion is for. It is careful and it is yours. The attentive few read it three times. Two letters come, one grateful and one not, and the secretary takes both calls and puts them on your desk without comment. {@pastor}, back, reads it in the car and says it was fine, which from him is a sentence.

choices.label: Write something worth reading, in a voice that is plainly not his
choices.outcome: You write about the parish's founding, which you have looked up, and about the family whose name is on the bell, whose grandchildren are still in the pews and did not know. It is the first column in eleven years that has been cut out and kept. The pastor reads it and is, for a moment, a man whose vicar has done something he cannot do, and you both see him decide how to feel about that.

events.title: The Schedule
events.body: {@pastor} wants to drop the Sunday 7:00. He has wanted to for years. The 7:00 draws sixty people in a church that seats six hundred, most of them over seventy, all of them certain, and the two of you say five Masses between Saturday evening and Sunday noon, and neither of you preaches well by the fifth. He has decided that this is the year, and he has decided, because he is not a fool, that the announcement should come from you. A new priest can say it is for the good of the whole parish. A pastor of eleven years saying it is a man breaking a promise. He puts it to you at dinner as a thing already settled and asks how you would like to handle the pastoral council, which will object, and the letters, which will come, and the woman who has attended the 7:00 since 1974 and whose husband is buried under the window she looks at. It is the right decision. It is also his, and he is handing you the part of it that hurts.
events.flavorPrompt: The arithmetic of Masses against the sixty who come at seven. The pastor hands over the part that hurts.

choices.label: Announce it, take the letters, and say it is for the whole parish
choices.outcome: You say it from the pulpit at all five Masses on one Sunday and you do not blame the pastor and you do not make it sound easy. The letters come. The woman from 1974 does not speak to you for a year and then, at her own husband's anniversary Mass, does. The pastoral council grumbles and folds. {@pastor} owes you and knows it, and the chancery hears that you can carry a hard thing.

choices.label: Tell him you will support it, but it has to come from him
choices.outcome: He does not like it. He says it anyway, badly, at the 7:00 only, in a voice that makes it sound like a punishment, and the letters go to the bishop instead of to you. He is angry with you for a month for being right. The 7:00 dies in Advent. The sixty scatter to the 8:30 and to the parish across the river, and the ones who stay know you did not do it.

choices.label: Offer to take the 7:00 yourself, every week, with no homily and no music
choices.outcome: A Low Mass in all but name: twenty-five minutes, the readings, three sentences, no organist. The sixty accept it as a mercy. {@pastor} accepts it as a delay and says the problem will still be there when you are gone, and he is right, but for now the parish keeps its 7:00 and you keep your Sunday from seven until two, and something in you likes it.

events.title: The One O'Clock
events.body: The Spanish Mass at {parish} is at one in the afternoon because that was the slot nobody wanted when it was added, and it now draws more people than the 8:30 and the 10:30 together. The families stand in the side aisles. The parking lot is full at half past twelve and the 11:00 people cannot get out. {@pastor} does not have the language and has a deacon who does, and a rotating list of priests from the deanery who come when they can. The Spanish community has asked, through the deacon, through three families, and now through a letter with two hundred signatures, for the 10:30. The 10:30 people have been at the 10:30 since the church was built and gave the money for the roof. This is not a question about a time slot. It is the question of which parish this is now, and the pastor, who is a decent man, has put it in a drawer for four years because every answer loses him something. This week the letter has been copied to the chancery, and {@pastor} takes it out of the drawer and hands it to you.
events.flavorPrompt: Two congregations under one roof. Parking, side aisles, a letter with signatures. No villains.

choices.label: Recommend the swap and offer to preach it to the 10:30 people yourself
choices.outcome: You stand in front of the people who paid for the roof and tell them the church is full at one and half empty at half ten, and that the parish is one parish. Half of them believe you. A dozen leave for the parish across the river. The Spanish Mass moves to 10:30 in September and the side aisles are clear, and the diocese notes that {parish} made a decision.

choices.label: Recommend adding a second Spanish Mass instead of moving one
choices.outcome: A Saturday evening Mass in Spanish, which nobody asked for and which solves the parking and not the question. It draws four hundred by Advent. The deanery list of Spanish-speaking priests gets thinner, because you have added a Mass to it. {@pastor} is relieved. The letter-writers are polite about it and understand exactly what has happened, and so does the chancery.

choices.label: Take the one o'clock yourself, every week, in Spanish, and let the schedule question wait
choices.outcome: The community has never had the same priest two weeks running. Within two months they have your name, your homily habits, and your mother's town, and the letter stops mattering because the thing under the letter was a wish to belong to a priest. The 10:30 question is still in the drawer. You have bought the pastor time and bought yourself a parish inside the parish, and both of those have consequences.

events.title: The Council
events.body: The pastoral council at {parish} meets on the third Thursday in the school library, twelve people and the pastor, and it has an agenda that is a photocopy of last year's agenda with the dates changed. {@pastor} presides the way a man holds an umbrella: it is a thing he does so the rain does not reach him. Nothing is decided at council because nothing is brought to it that requires deciding. The festival committee reports. The finance council chair reads a figure. Someone raises the parking again. You are there because vicars attend, and you have made the mistake, in your second meeting, of asking a question about the school subsidy that was clear, specific, and answerable. The room went quiet the way a room does when it has seen something rare. Now the chair has asked, in an email copied to the pastor, whether you would consider taking on the strategic planning subcommittee, which does not exist, and a woman who used to run a hospital has asked whether you would meet her for coffee about the parish's five-year picture. You have been noticed. The noticing has a cost.
events.flavorPrompt: The umbrella pastor. The specific danger of being competent in a room that was not expecting it.

choices.label: Take the subcommittee and make it real
choices.outcome: By spring it meets monthly, has a written parish profile, and has produced the first honest picture of the school's finances anyone has drawn. It eats a night a week. {@pastor} is pleased and slightly alarmed, and the chancery, which reads council minutes when they are worth reading, notes your name. You are becoming the man who does this, and that is a door that opens onto committees.

choices.label: Decline, and say your first years are for the sick and the pulpit
choices.outcome: The chair is disappointed and the hospital woman is not surprised. You go back to being the vicar who sits at the end of the table. The question about the subsidy is not asked again by anyone, and the figure in it gets worse. You have kept your evenings and your reputation as a pastor rather than a manager, and you have watched a thing you could have fixed go unfixed.

choices.label: Meet the hospital woman for coffee, and keep the council at arm's length
choices.outcome: She is the most capable lay person in the parish and she has been waiting years for a priest who would let her be. You give her nothing official and an hour a month, and she gives you a picture of {parish} that the council has never seen. It goes into a drawer. The drawer will be useful. The council stays a photocopy, and you have a friend in it.

events.title: The Festival
events.body: The {parish} festival is three days in late summer, a raffle, rides on the school lot, and a beer tent that clears more than the raffle and the rides together. The festival committee has run it for twenty years and does not need a priest, except that a priest must be seen. {@pastor} is seen on Friday, in a polo shirt, for two hours, and then is not seen. You are the priest for the rest. There is a dunk tank and you are in it at four on Saturday. There is a beer tent and the committee chair, a man who has given more to this parish than anyone alive, stands you a drink at nine and then another, and the tent is loud and warm and the whole parish is there in its summer clothes and nobody, for three days, is dying or divorcing or asking about the assessment. It is the best the parish is at being a parish and it is also a place where a priest who is watched can be watched, and you know before the second glass which kind of night this is going to be.
events.flavorPrompt: Late summer, a beer tent, a dunk tank. Warmth and exposure together.

choices.label: Be there for all of it, take the dunk tank, take the one drink and stop
choices.outcome: You are wet by five and dry by seven and you know a hundred more faces by Sunday night. The one drink is enough and the chair notices you stop, and respects it. The committee clears forty thousand and says so at the 10:30, and the pastor, who was seen for two hours, gets the thanks. You did the thing vicars do. You are tired for a week.

choices.label: Stay in the tent until it closes
choices.outcome: It is a good night. It is a very good night. You are the priest who stayed, who sang the second verse, who the committee talks about for a month. You are also the priest whom the housekeeper had to hear come in at one, and the one a woman from the 8:30 saw, and described, and you learn in the fall that she described it to the pastor.

effects.value: Seen drinking late at the parish festival

choices.label: Work the tent all weekend, and drink nothing
choices.outcome: The chair stands you a drink and you take a lemonade and he looks at you for a second and then nods, because his brother did the same thing for thirty years. You pour for three nights and hear everything. The tent is where the parish tells the truth, and you are the only one in it who will remember on Monday. You come out of it with a list of people to visit and a reputation that a chair with a brother will carry for you.

events.title: The Count
events.body: The Sunday collection at {parish} is counted on Monday morning by two teams of retired parishioners who have done it for years, in the office with the door closed, and the totals are entered on a sheet the secretary types and the pastor signs. That is the system and it is the system in most parishes and it works on trust. This Monday one of the counters is in the hospital and {@secretary} asks if you would sit in, and you do, with a coffee, and you watch. You see the envelopes opened and stacked and the loose cash sorted. You see the sheet. And you see, because you are new and have not learned not to see, that the loose cash goes into a bank bag before it is counted, and that the bag goes to the secretary's desk, and that the figure on the sheet for loose cash is a round number, and that the counters do not look at each other when it happens. It may be nothing. It may be a habit twenty years old with nobody left who remembers why. It may be the thing that, three pastors from now, is the story of this parish. The counters are packing up. The secretary is asking if you want another coffee.
events.flavorPrompt: A Monday count in a closed office. The player sees something that may be nothing. No accusation in the prose.

choices.label: Say nothing. You are new and it may be nothing
choices.outcome: You drink the second coffee. The sheet is signed. It is, you tell yourself, a system that predates you and will outlast you, and a vicar who accuses the office in his first year is a vicar who is moved. You do not forget the bag. You notice, in the weeks after, that you are watching the secretary's desk, and that she has noticed you watching.

effects.value: Saw an irregularity in the collection count and did not raise it

choices.label: Describe what you saw to {@pastor} that evening, without a conclusion
choices.outcome: He listens with his eyes on the television. He says the bag is for the safe, that the loose cash has been rounded since before the secretary's time because the counters cannot agree on coins, and that he trusts her. Then he says, after a moment, that he will have a look. He does not say when. You have said it to the man whose job it is, and you have made him uncomfortable in his own house.

choices.label: Ask to see the deposit slip against the sheet, and keep your own tally
choices.outcome: You ask lightly, as a man interested in how things work, and the secretary shows you the slip, and it does not match the sheet by an amount that could be coins or could not. You write the two figures in a notebook with the date. You do it for six Mondays. By the sixth you have a pattern or a coincidence, written down in your hand, and you have not yet decided which, or what a vicar does with a notebook.

events.title: The Auditor
events.body: The diocese sends an internal auditor to each parish on a cycle, and this year the cycle reaches {parish}. He is a layman in a grey suit with a laptop and a checklist and a manner of great patience, and he sits in the school library for four days with the ledgers and the deposit slips and the count sheets going back three years. {@secretary} brings him coffee. {@pastor} is cordial and elsewhere. On the third day the auditor asks whether he might have twenty minutes with the vicar, which is on the checklist, and you sit across from him and he asks the ordinary questions: whether you have signing authority, whether you have ever been asked to sign a count sheet, whether you are aware of any parish accounts not on the list in front of him. Then he asks whether there is anything about the parish's financial procedures you would like to tell him, and he waits, and he is a man who has learned to wait. What you saw on that Monday is in the room. He does not know it is there. The question is whether it leaves the room with him.
events.flavorPrompt: A grey suit, a laptop, and a question left open on purpose. The weight of the pause.

choices.label: Tell him what you saw, as exactly as you can
choices.outcome: He writes it down without expression and asks two questions that tell you he has seen it before. The audit letter, a month later, recommends that loose cash be counted before bagging and that the pastor rotate count teams. The secretary reads the letter and knows where it came from. The pastor reads it and says nothing to you for a week. Nothing is proven. The system is changed. That is what an audit is for.

choices.label: Hand him the notebook
choices.outcome: Six Mondays, two columns, dated. He reads it in silence, photographs each page, and hands it back. The audit stays a week longer. The letter, when it comes, goes to the bishop as well as the pastor, and a diocesan finance officer visits, and the secretary retires in the spring with a card and a cake and no explanation. Nobody ever tells you what the numbers were. The chancery knows your name for a reason it will not say.

choices.label: Say you have nothing to add. It is the pastor's parish
choices.outcome: He nods and closes the laptop. The audit letter finds the books in order. The bag goes to the secretary's desk every Monday for the rest of your time here, and you know it does, and the auditor's twenty minutes sit in your memory as the moment you decided to be a man things are not said to. If it is ever found, the file will show you were asked.

effects.value: Told a diocesan auditor there was nothing to report after seeing a count irregularity

choices.label: Say the pastor has already been told and refer the auditor to him
choices.outcome: It is true and it is the correct channel and it puts the question on the desk of the man who put it in a drawer. The auditor has the conversation with {@pastor}, who has, it turns out, had a look, and found the rounding, and stopped it, and not mentioned it to you. The letter is mild. The secretary is cooler with everyone. You went through the pastor and the pastor, for once, had gone through.

events.title: The Loft and the Classroom
events.body: {@dre} runs the religious education program at {parish} out of the school basement on Wednesday nights and Sunday mornings, two hundred children and forty volunteer catechists, and she has done it for nine years on a salary that would embarrass a diocese with more shame. {@music_director} runs the choir, the cantors, the funeral music, and a children's choir that rehearses on Wednesday nights in the church, which is above the basement, and which needs, for the children's choir, the same children. That is the war. It has been going on for three years in the form of emails copied to the pastor, who does not read email, and it has now arrived on your desk in the form of both of them, separately, on the same afternoon, each asking you to speak to the other. The First Communion Mass is in six weeks. The DRE wants it plain and the children in the front pews. The music director wants the children's choir in the loft, which means half the First Communicants in surplices facing away from their parents. Neither of them is wrong. Both of them are tired. The pastor, told about it, says that this is what a vicar is for.
events.flavorPrompt: Two competent, underpaid people who need the same children. The pastor absent by choice.

choices.label: Back the DRE: the children stay in the pews with their families
choices.outcome: The First Communion is plain and the parents can see their children, and the DRE, who has not been backed by a priest in three years, cries in the basement afterward where she thinks nobody is. The music director takes it as a verdict on nine years of work and starts looking, quietly, at a parish across the diocese with a better organ. Wednesday nights become peaceful and a little thinner.

choices.label: Back the music director: a First Communion Mass should sound like something
choices.outcome: The children sing from the loft and it is, genuinely, beautiful, and half the parents watch the backs of their children's heads and take photographs of the organ pipes. The music director tells the choir that finally somebody understands. The DRE reschedules her Wednesday sessions to Tuesdays and loses eleven catechists who cannot do Tuesdays, and does not tell you, and you find out from the secretary in the fall.

choices.label: Put them in a room with you and a calendar and do not let anyone out until Wednesday nights are solved
choices.outcome: It takes three hours and one of them nearly leaves. You come out with a rotation: children's choir on the first and third Wednesdays, catechesis on the second and fourth, First Communion with the choir in the front pews, facing sideways, which satisfies nobody and works. They do not become friends. They stop copying the pastor. You have spent an evening and bought yourself two staff who will, from now on, come to you first, which is not always a gift.

choices.label: Tell them both that this is the pastor's decision and walk it back to his desk
choices.outcome: You are correct and it changes nothing. {@pastor} listens to both of them for ten minutes and says do what you did last year, and last year the war was already three years old. The DRE and the music director each decide, separately, that you are no use, and the First Communion is a compromise that everybody resents. You have kept out of it, which is a thing vicars are told to do and are never thanked for.

events.title: The Estimate
events.body: The parish has three estimates for the church roof, which is the diocesan minimum, and {@pastor} has put them in a folder and asked you to read them because you are, he says, the one who reads things. The three are from three contractors and they are for sixty, ninety, and one hundred and forty thousand dollars, and the pastor intends to take the sixty, because it is sixty. {@maintenance}, who has been on that roof more times than any of the three contractors, tells you in the boiler room, where he tells you things, that the sixty is a man who will patch and paper and be gone by the time it leaks, that the ninety is honest and will do it right, and that the one-forty is the finance council chair's brother-in-law and has always bid high on this parish because he knows the pastor takes the low one and nobody looks at the middle. He says it without heat. He has said it before, to other vicars, and watched the sixty get taken. The finance council meets Thursday. The pastor will present the sixty as prudence. The maintenance man is not on the finance council, and has never been asked to be.
events.flavorPrompt: The boiler room as the confessional of the parish's buildings. Three numbers and what each one really means.

choices.label: Let the pastor take the sixty. It is his parish and his roof
choices.outcome: The finance council approves it in four minutes. The work is done by October and it looks fine from the ground. {@maintenance} says nothing to you about it, which is its own sentence. The roof will leak again in three winters, and by then it may be somebody else's problem, and the parish will have saved thirty thousand dollars it will spend twice.

choices.label: Make the case for the ninety at the finance council, with the maintenance man's reasons and not his name
choices.outcome: You say it plainly: the low bid is a patch and the parish will pay for the roof twice. The chair, whose brother-in-law is the high bid, supports you with unexpected warmth. {@pastor} is outvoted in his own council for the first time in years and takes it badly for a month. The roof is done right. The maintenance man, when you tell him, says only that it was about time somebody read the middle one.

choices.label: Go up on the roof with him and write your own scope of work for the council
choices.outcome: Two hours on a ladder and a page of notes. The scope you write asks the sixty to quote on the same terms as the ninety, and the sixty comes back at eighty-five, which tells the council everything. The ninety gets the job at eighty-seven. {@pastor} is impressed and slightly uneasy at having a vicar who can read a roof. The maintenance man has, for the first time, a priest who has stood where he stands.

events.title: The Glass at Eleven
events.body: You come in late from the hospital and the light is on in the pastor's study. The door is half open. {@pastor} is at his desk with the lamp on and no papers on it and a glass, and the bottle beside the glass, and he is not reading and he is not praying and he is not asleep. He looks up and says good night in the voice of a man who has been having the same conversation with himself for some hours. You have seen the wine at dinner and the second glass and the third. This is different. This is a man who drinks alone at eleven with the door half open because he has stopped caring whether it is closed. In the morning he says the 8:30 well, hears confessions, meets the funeral director, and is fine, and is fine every day, and you begin to understand that fine is what a man can be for years. The housekeeper knows. The secretary knows. The presbyterate, you suspect, knows and has decided that he is a good pastor, which he is, and that the rest is his business, which it is until the night it is not. You are the only one who lives in the house.
events.flavorPrompt: A study at eleven, a lamp, a half-open door. Do not moralize. The competence of a man who is fine every day.

choices.label: Say good night and close his door behind you
choices.outcome: You close it gently. You do not sleep for a while. In the weeks after you notice the bottle level and the recycling and the nights the light is on, and you notice him noticing that you notice, and neither of you says a word, and the house goes on. You are keeping his secret, which is what the house has always done, and you are now part of the house.

choices.label: Go in, sit down, and ask him how long
choices.outcome: He looks at you for a long moment and then tells you. Since his mother died, or since the last vicar, or since the bishop moved his friend, the story moves as he tells it and you let it. He does not promise anything and you do not ask him to. You have become the one person in {parish} who has said it out loud to him. He will either forgive you for that or he will not, and it may take a year to learn which.

choices.label: Tell him, from your own history, what you see
choices.outcome: You tell him when you stopped and why and what it looked like from inside. He does not argue, because a man who drinks alone at eleven knows what it looks like from inside. He asks whether you go to meetings. You tell him. He says he is too old for church basements and then laughs, because of where he works. He does not stop. But there is now a man in his house who has said the true thing without contempt, and he starts leaving the study door closed.

events.title: The Funeral He Could Not Say
events.body: It is a Saturday in {parish} and {@pastor} has a ten o'clock funeral, a family he has known for thirty years, and at half past nine he has not come down. You go up. He is dressed and sitting on the edge of the bed and he is not fit to say it, and he knows he is not, and he looks at you with the expression of a man who has been waiting some years for this particular morning. The funeral director is in the sacristy. The family is in the front pews. The organist is playing the prelude for the second time. You have twenty minutes to say a funeral Mass for people you have never met, for a woman whose name you have to ask, and you have the rest of your life to decide what you do about the man upstairs. The housekeeper is in the hall with her hands folded. She has seen this before. That is what her face says. She has seen it before and it was handled, and it can be handled again, and she is waiting to see whether you are the kind of priest who handles things.
events.flavorPrompt: Twenty minutes, a prelude playing twice, a family in the pews. The housekeeper's folded hands.

choices.label: Say the funeral, and on Monday call {@vicar_for_clergy}
choices.outcome: You say it well enough. The family thanks you and asks after Father. On Monday you make the call, and the vicar for clergy is not surprised, which tells you something about how long this has been known and not acted upon. {@pastor} goes away in the spring for three months to a place the diocese uses and comes back grey and sober and a stranger to you. He never asks who called. He knows. It is the right thing and it costs you the house.

choices.label: Say the funeral, and tell the family he was called to the hospital
choices.outcome: The family believes you, because why would they not. The housekeeper unfolds her hands. He comes down at two, showered, and thanks you in a voice you have not heard from him, and you are now the vicar who covers, which is a thing this house has needed and a thing the house does to its vicars. It happens twice more that year. Each time is easier to explain and harder to carry.

effects.value: Covered for a pastor who could not say a funeral for drink

choices.label: Say the funeral, and that evening tell him it is the diocese or a doctor, and he chooses
choices.outcome: He chooses the doctor, because you have given him the choice and because you have said it before without contempt and he believes you will make the call. He goes to a physician in the city who has treated priests for twenty years and does not report to the chancery. It is not a cure. It is a man with a vicar who will not lie for him and will not inform on him, and that turns out to be the thing he needed, or nearly.

events.title: The Pastor's Heart
events.body: {@pastor} has been short of breath on the stairs since Lent and has said it is the stairs. In June he sits down halfway through the 8:30 homily and finishes it sitting, and the parish notices, and at dinner he tells you it was the heat. The following week his physician, who is a parishioner, calls the rectory and asks for you, not him, and says with the care of a man breaking a confidence for a reason that Father has an appointment for a stress test he has cancelled twice, and that a third time would be unwise. The pastor is sixty-eight. He has run {parish} for eleven years and there is nobody, in his mind, who could take it, and if he is off for six weeks the bishop will send an administrator, and administrators, in his experience, become pastors. He is not afraid of dying. He is afraid of being replaced while alive. You are the man in the house, and the physician has called you, and the pastor's next appointment is Thursday and he has not told the secretary to hold the morning.
events.flavorPrompt: The fear of being replaced while alive. A physician who calls the vicar. No melodrama.

choices.label: Tell him the physician called, and that you will drive him Thursday
choices.outcome: He is furious at the physician and then, briefly, at you, and then he gets in the car. The test is bad enough. There is a stent in August and six weeks of you saying every Mass in the parish and the chancery sending nobody, because you asked them not to and {@vicar_for_clergy} was, for once, persuadable. He comes back thinner and grateful and still the pastor. You are exhausted and you have his trust in a way you did not before.

choices.label: Call {@vicar_for_clergy} and let the diocese make him go
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy is kind about it and firm, and an administrator is appointed for the summer, a monsignor from the chancery who is efficient and cold. The pastor has his stent and his six weeks and comes back to a parish that has learned it can run without him, which is the thing he feared. He does not blame you aloud. The parish, which liked the monsignor's short homilies, is briefly and disloyally cheerful.

choices.label: Read the situation as a physician would, and tell him what a cancelled stress test means
choices.outcome: You tell him what you know about men of sixty-eight who get short of breath on stairs, and you say it without softening because you were once paid not to soften it. He hears it as a diagnosis rather than a nag and goes on Thursday by himself. The stent is in July. He tells the parish from the pulpit, which he would not have done, and the parish prays for him, which he had not expected to want.

choices.label: Say nothing. He is a grown man and it is his heart
choices.outcome: He cancels the third time. He is fine through the summer and fine in the fall, and then in Advent he is not, and it is an ambulance during the 8:30 and the parish sees that too. He survives it. The physician does not call you again. You learn what it costs to be a man who respects another man's choices, which is that you get to watch them.

events.title: The Saint and the Ledger
events.body: {@pastor} is, by any measure the parish uses, a holy man. He is in the church at five. He visits the dying and stays. He has given away, the secretary says, most of what he has been paid for thirty years, and the people of {parish} know it and would follow him into a fire. He also has not opened the diocesan finance office's letters since February. You find them in his study when he asks you to look for a baptismal certificate: eleven envelopes, unopened, and a twelfth that he did open, which says that the parish is four months behind on the assessment and that the school subsidy will be withheld until the annual report is filed, and that the report is now nine months late. He has not told anyone. He would not know how. The finance council has not met since the chair moved to Arizona. The bookkeeper comes on Thursdays and does what she is asked, and she has not been asked. This is not theft and it is not malice. It is a man who believes that God will provide and who has been, for thirty years, right, and who has now been sent a vicar who can read a balance sheet.
events.flavorPrompt: Holiness and eleven unopened envelopes. The pastor is not a fool; he is a man with one gift.

choices.label: Open the envelopes, file the report, and tell no one it was you
choices.outcome: It takes three weeks of evenings and the bookkeeper's Thursdays. The report goes in with his signature. The assessment gets a payment plan. The subsidy is released. The finance office, which knows exactly who wrote this, writes his name on the letter and yours on a list. He never asks how it was fixed and would not understand if you told him. You have done the thing he cannot do, and you have become the man who does it.

choices.label: Put the twelve envelopes on the dinner table and open them with him
choices.outcome: He reads each one and puts it down and looks at you like a man being shown a wound he had decided not to feel. He asks what he should do. You tell him, in order. He does about half of it and you do the rest and the report is filed by Advent, late, with a note from him that the finance office finds moving and files anyway. He is grateful in a way that costs him. He is also, for the first time, a little afraid of you.

choices.label: Call the diocesan finance office yourself and tell them what you found
choices.outcome: They send someone. She is competent and kind and she treats the pastor like a beloved grandfather who has left the stove on. A finance council is appointed from the chancery's list. The report is filed. The parish learns its saint cannot count and loves him anyway, and the chancery learns that the vicar at {parish} will call them, which they file under useful, and the pastor learns it too.

choices.label: Put the envelopes back. It is his parish, and God has provided so far
choices.outcome: You find the certificate and close the drawer. The subsidy is withheld in the spring and the school lets a teacher go, and the parish does not connect the two, and the pastor prays about it. The finance office, in June, sends a man instead of a letter. You were not the one who fixed it and you were not the one who broke it, and you have learned what it feels like to have been able to.

events.title: The Opened Envelope
events.body: The mail at {parish} comes to the office and the secretary sorts it, and yours is left on the hall table. In October a letter from the chancery, addressed to you by name, is on the table with the flap open and pressed shut again, not well. It is nothing: a notice about a study day. But it has been read. You watch for a week and it happens again, a letter from a classmate this time, and you understand that {@pastor} reads the vicar's mail, and has for years, and that the last vicar knew and the housekeeper knows and it is simply a thing the house does. His reasons, if you asked, would be good ones. A vicar is his responsibility. The chancery writes to vicars about pastors. A young man alone can get into trouble and a pastor should see it coming. He is not a malicious man. He is a man who believes that there is nothing in his house he is not entitled to know, and you are in his house, and the question is whether you say so and what it costs to be a man who says so.
events.flavorPrompt: The pressed-shut flap. The pastor's reasons are real and the violation is real. Both.

choices.label: Tell him, at dinner, that you have noticed and that it stops
choices.outcome: He does not deny it and does not apologize. He says a pastor has a duty and you say a priest has a right, and neither of you gives ground, and the mail on the hall table is sealed from then on. He is cold for a month. The housekeeper tells the secretary that you stood up to him, and the secretary tells no one, and it is known anyway, and some of the parish likes it.

choices.label: Get a post office box in town and say nothing
choices.outcome: Your mail goes to a box by the hardware store and the hall table gets catalogues. He notices within a month, because he notices things, and says nothing, because saying something would require admitting why. It is a quiet war and you have won it quietly, and the price is that you both know you did not trust him enough to say so.

choices.label: Let him read it. You have nothing to hide and he is the pastor
choices.outcome: You decide that a man who reads your mail will learn nothing but that you are what you appear to be, and you write your letters accordingly, which is a discipline. He reads them for a year and stops, because they are dull, or because he trusts you now, and you do not know which. The classmates who write to you learn to call instead.

events.title: He Tells You First
events.body: {@pastor} asks you to walk with him after the 8:30, which he has never done, around the block and past the school, and on the second side of the block he says that {@bishop} has asked him to take a parish in the north of the diocese in June, and that he has said yes because there was no other answer, and that nobody at {parish} knows. Not the secretary. Not the staff. Not the finance council chair, who will take it personally. He is telling you because you live in the house and because you will be here when the new man comes and because, he says, looking at the school, a man should tell one person. He asks you to say nothing until the chancery announces it, which will be six weeks. Six weeks in which the secretary will ask you why he is cleaning out his files, the DRE will ask you about the fall program, and the presbyterate, which hears everything, will ask you at the deanery lunch whether the rumor is true. He has given you a thing to carry. It is the first time he has treated you as a brother priest and it is, you realize on the third side of the block, also the last thing he will ask of you as your pastor.
events.flavorPrompt: A walk around the block. The confidence as an act of trust and a burden. The school in view.

choices.label: Promise to keep it, and keep it
choices.outcome: Six weeks of being asked and not answering. The secretary knows by the fourth week, because she is the secretary, and knows you knew, and forgives you for it, barely. At the deanery lunch you say you have heard nothing, which is a lie of a kind priests tell each other and forgive. When the letter is read at all Masses in May, {@pastor} looks at you across the sanctuary, once. You have kept it.

choices.label: Promise to keep it from the parish, but tell him you will not lie to the chancery if asked
choices.outcome: He looks at you for a moment and then nods, because it is fair, and because a man who is being moved knows what the chancery asks and of whom. You keep it from the parish. The chancery, when it calls, gets the truth and no more. He says, on the last night in the house, that you were the only one who told him the terms first.

choices.label: Keep it from everyone but the secretary, who will need the six weeks
choices.outcome: You tell her on Monday, in her office, with the door closed, and she is silent for a long moment and then opens a drawer and takes out a list she has kept for exactly this. The transition is the smoothest the parish has had. {@pastor} finds out she knew, in the last week, and knows who told her, and does not raise it, and it sits between you like a stone at the table.

events.title: The Call from the Chancery
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} calls the rectory on a Tuesday and asks for you, and asks whether you have fifteen minutes, and the fifteen minutes are about {@pastor}. The tone is friendly and the questions are careful. How is he, generally. How has the parish been, this year. Has he seemed tired. Has he spoken to you about his future. The vicar for clergy does not say why he is asking and does not need to, because you know that the bishop is moving him, and now you know something else: that the chancery is deciding whether the move is a promotion or a kindness or a removal, and that they are asking the man who lives in the house. The pastor asked you to say nothing. He did not ask you to lie. But the questions are shaped so that the truth and silence sound the same, and the vicar for clergy is listening for the shape of your answers rather than the words, and every priest who has taken this call knows that what he says about his pastor is also what the chancery will remember about him. The line is quiet. He is waiting.
events.flavorPrompt: A phone call shaped so that truth and silence sound alike. The chancery listening for shape.

choices.label: Say he is well, the parish is well, and that you would not know about his future
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy thanks you and rings off, and you have kept the confidence and told the chancery, in effect, that you are a man who keeps them, which the chancery values and does not reward. The move goes ahead as planned. {@pastor} never knows the call was made. You know that the chancery has your name next to a question mark, and you know what the question was.

choices.label: Answer each question truly and volunteer nothing
choices.outcome: He is tired. The parish has been steady. He has mentioned his future, and you would rather he told the chancery himself what he said. The vicar for clergy hears the last answer for what it is and says, carefully, that this is helpful. The move goes ahead with a note in the file that the vicar at {parish} is straight, and another note, which you will never see, about whether straight is what they want.

choices.label: Tell him, because he is asking, about the nights the study light is on
choices.outcome: You say it as plainly as you can and it is the hardest sentence you have said to a chancery official. The vicar for clergy is silent for a moment and then says thank you in a different voice. The move is changed. He goes to a smaller parish with a resident retired priest, which is a kindness dressed as an assignment, and he knows why, and he knows who. The chancery writes your name in a column it keeps for men who tell them things.

choices.label: Tell the chancery what a pastor he has been, at length, and make the move a promotion
choices.outcome: You give the vicar for clergy eleven years in ten minutes: the dying he sat with, the school he kept open, the way the parish follows him. It is all true and it is also advocacy, and the vicar for clergy knows the difference and is moved anyway. The announcement, when it comes, calls the new assignment a recognition. {@pastor} hears the word and looks at you and does not ask.

events.title: After the Second Glass
events.body: It is a Sunday night and the two of you have eaten, and {@pastor} has had his glass and then the second, and he is talking about {@bishop}. He does not usually. Tonight he tells you about a priest, a friend of his from seminary, who had a complaint made against him twenty years ago that was investigated and found to be nothing, and who was moved anyway, quietly, to the far edge of the diocese, and who is still there. He tells you what the bishop said about it at the time and what the bishop has said since, and what he thinks the bishop actually believes, which is that a priest is a liability to be managed. He says this without heat, at his own table, to the man he lives with. Then he stops and looks at you and says that he has never said that to anyone, and that you are a young man with a career, and that you should forget it. He means both halves. You have been handed his private opinion of the man who assigns you both, and the question is not whether you will repeat it, because you will not. The question is whether you agree with him, and whether you say so, here, where it is safe, or where it is not.
events.flavorPrompt: The pastor's private verdict on the bishop, offered at his own table. The player's own answer is the choice.

choices.label: Tell him you have seen the same thing, and that you think he is right
choices.outcome: He nods slowly and pours you the second glass you had not asked for. From then on there is a thing between you that is not quite friendship and is more than the house: two priests who have said what they think about the bishop and know the other will not repeat it. It is the safest kind of honesty and it changes what you can say to each other about everything else.

choices.label: Say that a bishop who does not manage liabilities is a bishop who ends up in the newspaper
choices.outcome: He looks at you as though you have said something he had hoped not to hear and has heard before. He says you may be right, and that you will go far, and does not mean the second as a compliment. The subject does not come up again. You have told the truth as you see it and it has cost you something at the table that you cannot name.

choices.label: Ask him what the friend would say, if asked
choices.outcome: He is quiet for a while. Then he says the friend would say he had been treated justly by an unjust process, and that he had made his peace, and that the peace was the worst part. You do not offer an opinion and he does not ask for one. He tells you the friend's name. It is a name you will hear again, in a very different room, and you will know something then that nobody else at the table does.

choices.label: Say that you would rather not know what he thinks of the bishop, and mean it kindly
choices.outcome: He takes it well, better than you expected: he says that is the correct answer and that he wishes he had given it at your age. The subject closes. You have kept yourself clean of an opinion you may have anyway, and you have told him, without saying it, that there is a line in you the house does not cross. He respects the line and does not love it.

events.title: The Week Alone
events.body: {@pastor} goes on retreat for a week, which he does every year, and this is the first year there has been a vicar to leave in charge. He leaves a page of notes on the kitchen table: the funeral home numbers, the alarm code, which parishioner will call about the Mass intentions and what to tell her, and at the bottom, in different ink, do not sign anything. Then he is gone, and the house is yours, and the parish is yours in the sense that everything that goes wrong in it for seven days will be yours. On Tuesday the boiler man comes and wants a decision. On Wednesday a family calls about a funeral for a man who left the Church in 1979 and wants a full Mass and a eulogy by his daughter who left it in 1998. On Thursday a woman comes to the office and asks to see the pastor and, told he is away, asks to see you, and closes the door, and begins to cry, and what she tells you is a matter for the chancery, not the parish. On Friday the secretary asks you to sign the payroll. It is what a pastor's week is, and you have five days of it, and no one to ask.
events.flavorPrompt: Seven days of a pastor's week, compressed. Do not name what the woman says; the player learns it is a chancery matter.

choices.label: Handle all of it, sign the payroll, and tell him about the woman when he is back
choices.outcome: The boiler gets a temporary fix. The funeral gets a Mass and a eulogy at the graveside, not the altar, and the daughter is angry and then is not. The payroll goes out. The woman's matter goes to the chancery on Monday with a note in your hand. {@pastor} comes back to a parish that ran, reads the note, and says only that you did right, and looks at you differently at dinner.

choices.label: Do not sign anything. Hold everything that can be held until he is back
choices.outcome: The boiler man leaves a card. The funeral is put off a week and the family goes to another parish. The payroll is late and the DRE, who is paid biweekly and has a mortgage, is not gracious about it. The woman's matter you take to the chancery yourself, because that could not wait, and you were right. He comes back to a parish that stopped and says nothing, which is his way of saying he expected it.

choices.label: Call {@brother_priest} for the funeral, the secretary for the payroll, and take the woman yourself
choices.outcome: The brother priest comes and says the funeral with a grace that comes from not being responsible for the family afterward. The secretary, it turns out, has been signing payroll with a stamp for years and shows you. The woman you take to the chancery on Friday, in your car, because she asked you to. You have discovered what a pastor's week is made of: other people's competence, arranged. He comes back and sees a parish that ran and does not know how.

events.title: The Attestation
events.body: The annual parish financial report to {diocese} carries an attestation that the parish finance council has reviewed it, with the names of the members and the date of the meeting. The finance council at {parish} has not met in two years. {@pastor} filled in a date. Now {@chancellor} has called, because the chancery is auditing attestations this year after a parish across the diocese turned out to have a finance council that did not exist, and the chancellor would like to confirm with someone other than the pastor that the meeting took place. The pastor asks you at dinner, without preamble, to take the call. He says the council would have approved it. He says the members are good men who will say they met if asked, which is probably true. He says that if the chancery decides he cannot run a finance council they will send someone to run it for him and that someone will be a stranger from the chancery in his parish office every Thursday until he dies. He says this looking at his plate. He has never asked you for anything before. The chancellor's office will call back tomorrow at ten.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor asking for one lie, to a man who has never asked before. The chancellor as a careful, ordinary caller.

choices.label: Tell him you will not say it, and that he should call the chancellor himself tonight
choices.outcome: He is silent for a long time. Then he gets up and goes to his study and you hear him on the phone, and it is a short call. The chancery sends a finance officer for six months, who is not a stranger for long. He does not forgive you for a year, and then he does, and tells you at the end of it that you were the only one in the house who would have said no. It is not a compliment and it is not an accusation.

choices.label: Take the call and say the council met
choices.outcome: The chancellor thanks you and moves to the next parish. The pastor says nothing at dinner and pours you a glass, which is his thanks. You have lied to the chancery for a man you live with, and it was a small lie about a meeting that should have happened, and every priest in the diocese has told one, and you know now that you are one of them. The finance council meets in March, because you make it.

effects.value: Confirmed a finance council meeting to the chancellor that did not take place

choices.label: Convene the finance council tonight, in the rectory, and let them review the report before ten tomorrow
choices.outcome: Four phone calls and three men in the parlor at eight with the report and a pot of coffee. They review it. It is a real meeting with real minutes, dated tonight. In the morning you tell the chancellor, exactly, that the council reviewed the report and that the date on the attestation was wrong and has been corrected. It is the truth and it is a rescue and the chancellor hears both. {@pastor} watches you do it and understands, for the first time, what a vicar can be for.

choices.label: Say you will not take the call, and leave what he tells the chancellor to him
choices.outcome: He takes the call himself and you do not ask what he said. The chancery, for whatever reason, moves on. You have not lied and you have not stopped him lying, and you have learned what that middle place feels like, which is that it is warm and nobody thanks you for standing in it. He is cooler with you for a season and then forgets, or decides to.

events.title: Twelve Minutes
events.body: {@pastor} preaches for seven minutes and has for years, and the parish is built around it: the 10:30 is out by 11:35, the parking lot clears before the 12:15, and the ushers can count on it. You preach for eighteen. You have been told this by three parishioners, two of them kindly, and now by the pastor, at breakfast, who says that the sacrament is the Mass and not the homily and that the people of {parish} have been formed to expect a certain shape to their Sunday, and that a man who breaks the shape should have a very good reason. He says twelve minutes, at most. He does not say it as a request. You have things to say. You have a doctrine of the Eucharist you have wanted to preach since Theology II, in three parts, and the third part is the one that matters and it comes at minute fourteen. You also have a parish that leaves after Communion and an usher who has started standing at the back with his arms folded at minute ten. Nobody is wrong here. The pastor is telling you what the parish can bear. The question is whether you believe him, and what you are preaching for.
events.flavorPrompt: An usher with folded arms at minute ten. The pastor's seven minutes as pastoral wisdom, not laziness.

choices.label: Cut to twelve and learn to say the third part first
choices.outcome: It takes a month and it makes you a better preacher, which you resent and then do not. The third part goes at minute three and the rest is illustration. The usher unfolds his arms. The pastor says nothing, which is his praise. You have learned that a homily is for the people in front of you and not for the professor in your head, and it costs you a little of what the professor gave you.

choices.label: Keep the eighteen. The parish can learn a new shape
choices.outcome: Some of it does. The 10:30 loses a few families to the 8:30 and gains a few from the parish across the river who have heard there is a priest here who says something. The usher complains to the pastor. The pastor says, at breakfast, that he told you, and does not tell you again. You have a following and a reputation and a parish divided by the clock, and the pastor's patience has a length you have now measured.

choices.label: Take the twelve and start a Tuesday night class for the three parts
choices.outcome: Twelve on Sunday and ninety minutes on Tuesday in the school library, for anyone who wants the rest of it. Twenty come the first week and forty by Advent. The pastor is satisfied and slightly bewildered. The parish has a shape on Sunday and a place on Tuesday for the people who wanted more, and you have a night a week you did not have and a reputation as a teacher that the chancery will remember when it wants one.

events.title: The Staff Party
events.body: The {parish} staff Christmas party is the second Thursday of Advent at an Italian restaurant the secretary chose eleven years ago and has not reconsidered, and it is the one night of the year the whole staff sits at one table: {@secretary}, {@dre}, {@music_director}, {@maintenance}, the bookkeeper, the school principal, the cook, the housekeeper, and the two of you. {@pastor} pays from a fund nobody audits. There is wine. There is a gift exchange with a limit that the music director always exceeds. By the second course the DRE is talking about the music director as though he were in another room, and the maintenance man is telling you what the boiler is really going to cost, and the housekeeper has had two glasses and is describing the last vicar's mother. It is warm and it is the parish's family dinner, with everything that means. The pastor gives a toast that is the same toast every year and everybody knows the ending. Then he looks at you and says, and now a word from the vicar, and the table turns, and you have not prepared one, and every person at that table will remember what you say next until you leave.
events.flavorPrompt: A long table at an Italian restaurant in Advent. Warmth, grievances, and one unprepared toast.

choices.label: Stand and say something true about each of them
choices.outcome: You go around the table. The secretary's nineteen years. The DRE's two hundred children. The music director's funerals. The maintenance man's ladder. It takes four minutes and the housekeeper cries, and the DRE and the music director look at each other for the first time all night. The pastor, who has never done it, is quiet for the rest of the meal. You have made the staff yours in a way that the pastor will notice.

choices.label: Say a short grace and a thank-you, and sit down
choices.outcome: Thirty seconds, a blessing, and the table goes back to its wine. It was the right length and nobody remembers it, which was the point. The pastor is pleased that you did not upstage him. The staff, who had wondered what you were, decide you are the quiet one, and the maintenance man goes back to the boiler, and the party is what it always is.

choices.label: Give the toast, and stay for the third bottle with the staff after the pastor leaves
choices.outcome: The pastor goes at nine and the table loosens. You hear, in the next two hours, everything: the DRE's real salary, the music director's job interview in the spring, what the secretary thinks of the finance council, and what the housekeeper thinks of you, which is better than you feared. You are one of them by midnight. The pastor hears about the third bottle and about midnight, and says nothing, and keeps it.

events.title: The Letter
events.body: The parish cannot afford the youth minister. This has been true for two years and {@pastor} has known it for two years and has kept her on because she is thirty-one and has a child and because the youth group, which is nine teenagers on a Sunday night, is the only thing at {parish} that is not older than he is. The finance council has said it in writing. The diocesan finance office has said it in a letter. Now the pastor has said it, at dinner, to you: she has to go by the end of June, and he would like you to tell her. He gives reasons. You are closer to her age. You have worked with the youth group. It will be less humiliating from a vicar than from the pastor who hired her. He does not give the real reason, which is that he cannot do it, and that he has never let anyone go in thirty years without leaving it to someone else, and that it is why the parish has a bookkeeper who cannot use the software and a cook for one man. She is in the office on Tuesday planning the summer retreat that will not happen. The letter, which the secretary has already typed, is in a folder on your desk.
events.flavorPrompt: The letter already typed. The pastor's incapacity is ordinary and human. The youth minister has a child.

choices.label: Tell her yourself, in person, with the letter and three months' notice you get the pastor to fund
choices.outcome: You go to the pastor first and get the three months, which he agrees to because it is money and not a conversation. Then you sit with her and say it plainly and stay for the anger and the tears and the question about the child. It is the worst hour of your year. She leaves in September with a reference you wrote and a job at a parish in the city. The nine teenagers scatter. You are now a man who has done this, and you will be asked to again.

choices.label: Tell him that he hired her and he will have to tell her
choices.outcome: He does not, for six weeks. Then the finance office calls again and he does it in the worst way, by memo, on a Friday, and she finds you in the sacristy and asks whether you knew, and you did. He is angry with you for making him and she is angry with you for not stopping him, and both are fair. The parish hears she was let go by memo and blames him, correctly, and the youth group ends.

choices.label: Find the money: cut the position to half time and fund it from the festival
choices.outcome: You take the festival surplus and the money the parish spends on a second bulletin printer and a line the pastor did not know existed, and you put together a half-time salary and take it to the finance council with a spreadsheet. They approve it because it is a spreadsheet. She takes the half time and the child's school hours and stays. The pastor is relieved beyond words and slightly embarrassed that it was possible.

events.title: The Principal's Numbers
events.body: The school principal at {parish} comes to the rectory on a weeknight, which she has never done, with a folder, and asks for you because {@pastor} is at a wake and because, she says, she has shown him the folder twice and he has prayed over it. The folder is enrollment.
