It is one hundred and forty-one children in a building built for three hundred, down nine from last year and eleven from the year before, and a tuition that has gone up every year to cover the loss and has, this year, caused the loss. There is a page of families who left and where they went. There is a page of what the parish subsidy actually covers, which is the heat. And there is a page, which she has not shown the pastor, on which she has worked out that the school has three years, and that the diocese will see it in two, and that when the diocese sees it the decision will be made in the chancery rather than in the parish. She wants a priest to know that. She wants, though she does not say it, a priest who will do something before the chancery does. The pastor loves the school. The pastor has prayed over the folder twice.
events.flavorPrompt: A folder, a weeknight, a principal who has done the arithmetic. The school as the parish's largest object.

choices.label: Take the third page to the pastor and make him read it aloud
choices.outcome: He reads it at the table and puts it down and is silent. Then he says that he will not be the pastor who closed the school, and you say that is exactly the choice, and he hears it. A committee is formed. It does what committees do, which is delay with dignity, but the delay has a plan in it now, and the chancery, when it looks, sees a parish that knows its own numbers, which buys a year.

choices.label: Spend the spring recruiting families yourself, at every Mass and every baptism
choices.outcome: You preach the school from the pulpit and mention it at every baptism and walk the Spanish Mass families through the tuition assistance form that nobody had translated. Enrollment goes up nineteen in September, the first rise in a decade. It is not enough and it is something, and the principal knows what it cost you, and the pastor tells the deanery that his vicar saved the school, which is not true yet.

choices.label: Take the folder to the diocesan schools office before they find it themselves
choices.outcome: The superintendent is grateful and pragmatic. A consultant comes. The word merger is used in a meeting for the first time, and the pastor learns of the meeting from the superintendent rather than from you, and does not forget it. The school gets a plan and a deadline. You have done the responsible thing and it has been noticed in the building where it matters, and in the house where it costs.

events.title: An Account Nobody Knew
events.body: A bank statement comes to the rectory addressed to {parish} Building Fund, an account {@pastor} has never heard of, at a bank the parish does not use, with a balance of eleven thousand dollars and a history of deposits going back six years and withdrawals, in cash, going back four. The statement came to the rectory by mistake; the address on the account is the parish office, and the office has been receiving them and someone in the office has been filing them somewhere that is not the file. The pastor, who opened it by accident, brings it to you at the dinner table and puts it beside your plate and says that he does not understand it, and he does not, and you do. Somebody with signing authority opened a parish account in the parish's name and has been moving money through it, and the money came from somewhere, and the list of people with signing authority is three names long and one of them is his. He asks you what he should do. He is asking because he is afraid of the answer and because it is a question about the people he has eaten with for a decade.
events.flavorPrompt: A bank statement beside a dinner plate. Three names. Do not identify the thief in the prose.

choices.label: Call the diocesan finance office in the morning, and tell him you will
choices.outcome: The finance office sends two people and a forensic accountant, and within a month the account is closed, the staff member is gone, and the diocese has decided not to prosecute because the parish's name would be in the paper. The pastor is interviewed twice and is cleared and looks ten years older. The parish is told the person left for family reasons. You did the thing the policy says and the policy was right and the house is quiet in a new way.

choices.label: Trace it yourself for a week before anyone is called, so the pastor knows what he is reporting
choices.outcome: A week with the statement, the count sheets, and the deposit slips, and you have it: which collection the money came from, when it started, and who was in the office on the days it moved. You give the pastor a page. He reads it and knows the name before he reaches it. He makes the call himself, with the page in front of him, and the finance office finds a parish that already knows. It ends the same way. He is not humiliated in the process, and he knows who spared him that.

choices.label: Tell him it is his to handle, and that you will support whatever he decides
choices.outcome: He handles it by calling the person into his study and having a conversation nobody else hears, and the account is closed the next week, and the person stays, and eleven thousand dollars is repaid over two years in cash in envelopes that go into the safe. The finance office never hears. It is mercy, or it is a pastor who could not bear the alternative, and you have supported it, and if it is ever found the file will show the vicar knew.

effects.value: Knew of a staff member's theft from a parish account and supported handling it in-house

events.title: The Room That Was His
events.body: Your room at {parish} was the last vicar's room, and the vicar before him, and before that it belonged for nine years to a priest whose name is not said in the house. The housekeeper will not say it. {@pastor}, asked, says that Father left the diocese and that it was before his time and that he has been asked by the chancery not to discuss it, which is true and is also the thing he says to end a conversation. Then a man comes to the office on a Wednesday afternoon, about forty, in work clothes, and asks for the pastor, and the pastor is out, and he asks for you. He says that he was an altar server here in the years the name is not said, and that he has been to the chancery, and that the chancery was correct and careful and gave him a number to call, and that nobody has asked him what happened in this building. He looks at the door to the rectory. He says he does not want money. He says he wants a priest to hear it, and that it should be one who lives in that room. You have been told the policy, which is that you listen and you report. He is waiting to see if you will do the first part.
events.flavorPrompt: A man in work clothes who will not sit down. The player listens; the abuse is named only as what he came to say. The policy is listen and report.

choices.label: Hear all of it, and tell him before he starts that you are required to report it, and will
choices.outcome: He says he knows. He talks for an hour. You do not interrupt and you do not console and you write nothing until he is gone. Then you call the victim assistance coordinator and {@vicar_for_clergy}, in that order, and the chancery's process, which was correct and careful, becomes a little less of a wall for one man because a priest in the building heard him. He does not come back. The pastor, told, goes very quiet, and moves you to a different room without being asked.

choices.label: Hear all of it, and ask him afterward what he wants the parish to do
choices.outcome: He wants his name said in the church where it happened, in a prayer, at a Mass, without the other name. You report it, as you must, and you take his request to the pastor, who is afraid of it and does it anyway, at a weekday Mass, with eleven people present and the man in the back pew. It changes nothing in the file. It changes the building. The chancery, told, is uneasy about the precedent and says nothing, and the pastor tells the deanery what his vicar asked for.

choices.label: Give him the pastor's number and the coordinator's number, and say you are not the right person
choices.outcome: He takes the numbers and looks at you for a moment and leaves. You tell the pastor, who is relieved and says you did right by the policy, which you did. The man does not call the pastor. The room is the same room. You have been the correct priest and you know, at night, that he came to see whether there was a different kind, and that you are not sure which kind you are.

events.title: The Triduum
events.body: On the Tuesday of Holy Week {@pastor} comes back from the Chrism Mass with a fever and by Wednesday night he cannot stand. The doctor says pneumonia and bed and there is no argument. {parish} has the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Thursday with the washing of feet and the procession to the altar of repose, the Passion on Friday at three and Stations at seven, the Vigil on Saturday with four adults to be baptized and six to be received, and five Masses on Easter Sunday, and it has one priest, and the priest is you. The deanery has nobody; every priest in {diocese} is saying his own Triduum. The music director has a program for each liturgy that runs to nine pages. The RCIA director has four catechumens who have waited a year and their sponsors and their families and a photographer. The sacristan has the fire for the Vigil and has never lit it without the pastor. It cannot all be done well. Some of it cannot be done at all. The pastor, from bed, in a voice you can barely hear, says to do what you can and let the rest go, and then says the Vigil is the one, and then coughs for a long time.
events.flavorPrompt: Holy Week with one priest. Accurate liturgy: Holy Thursday, Good Friday is not a Mass, the Vigil with the fire and the baptisms. The pastor's voice from the bed.

choices.label: Do all of it, and sleep in the sacristy between
choices.outcome: Thursday's feet, Friday's Passion, Stations, the fire, four baptisms, six receptions, and five Masses on Sunday with a homily written on Holy Saturday afternoon between the rehearsal and the Vigil. You are not sure you were present for any of it. The parish saw a priest who did not stop and will tell that story for a decade. On Easter Monday you cannot get out of bed and the pastor, who can now, brings you soup, and you do not know which of you is more surprised.

choices.label: Do the Triduum fully and cut Easter Sunday to three Masses
choices.outcome: The Vigil is the best liturgy you have ever been part of and the four baptisms are the reason you were ordained. Sunday has three Masses and the church is full for all of them, standing in the aisles, and the people who came to the cancelled 7:00 and 12:15 are angry in the parking lot and write to the bishop, and the bishop, who has been a pastor, ignores the letters. You did the thing the pastor said was the one.

choices.label: Call {@closest_classmate} and beg him to drive over after his own Vigil and take Easter morning
choices.outcome: He says yes before you finish asking. He drives ninety minutes after his own Vigil, sleeps four hours in the pastor's chair, and says the 7:00 and the 8:30 while you say the rest. The parish meets your friend and likes him. You have learned that the presbyterate is a thing you can call at midnight, and that you now owe a Triduum, and that you will pay it.

events.title: Easter Monday
events.body: The Octave begins and the parish empties. The lilies are still on the altar, going brown at the edges, and the church that was standing room on Sunday has nine people at the 6:30, and one of them is asleep. {@pastor} has gone, as he goes every Easter Monday, and will not be back until Wednesday. The secretary has taken the week. The office phone goes to the machine. You said, by your own count, eleven liturgies in four days, heard confessions for nine hours on Holy Saturday, and preached seven times, twice well. You have not read anything that was not a lectionary in a month. You have not called your mother since Laetare Sunday. The house is silent in the way a house is silent after a party, and there is a whole week of it, and the question of what a priest does with a week in which nothing is required of him turns out to be a harder question than any of the ones Holy Week asked. The breviary is on the table. So is the car key. So is a novel someone gave you at Christmas that you have not opened. It is nine in the morning and the day has no shape at all.
events.flavorPrompt: The emptiness after the Octave begins. Brown-edged lilies. A day with no shape.

choices.label: Sleep, walk, read the novel, and let the week be empty
choices.outcome: You sleep until ten for four days running. You finish the novel. You walk to the river and back and do not think about the parish for whole hours at a time, and by Thursday you are a man again rather than a function, and the 6:30 on Friday is said by someone who is present. The pastor, back on Wednesday, sees it and says nothing, which means he knows what it is.

choices.label: Drive to the monastery two hours north and make a private retreat until Wednesday
choices.outcome: The guest master gives you a room with a bed and a desk and a window onto a field. You go to the Hours with the monks and say nothing for three days. It is the first silence since Advent. You come back on Wednesday with the shape of the year restored and the sense, which the parish cannot give you, of being a very small part of something that was going on before you and will go on after.

choices.label: Use the week to catch up: the hospital list, the correspondence, the baptism prep backlog
choices.outcome: You clear the desk. Eleven hospital visits, forty letters, three baptism families who had been waiting since Lent. By Wednesday the parish is in better order than it has been since you arrived, and you are exactly as tired as you were on Monday, and you have not called your mother. The pastor comes back to a clean desk and does not ask what it cost.

events.title: The Mission Preacher
events.body: Every Lent {parish} has a three-night parish mission, a visiting preacher and a hall full of people who do not otherwise come on weeknights, and {@pastor} has this year invited a priest from another diocese whom he has known for forty years and who is, in the wider Church, a name: a man who wrote, two years ago, a public letter about how bishops handle allegations, and who named names, and whose own bishop has not forgiven him for it. {@bishop} has not said anything about the invitation. {@bishop} does not need to. The chancery has called the pastor to confirm the dates in a tone the pastor describes as informational. The mission is Monday to Wednesday. The pastor will introduce him on Monday. He asks you to introduce him on Tuesday, in front of a hall that will be fuller than Monday because of what will be said on Monday, and the introduction is a page you write yourself, and it can be a paragraph about a priest who preaches well or it can be about the letter. The man himself, at dinner on Sunday, is smaller and quieter than his letter and eats very little. He asks you what you think of it. He is not asking to be flattered.
events.flavorPrompt: A visiting preacher known for a public letter about bishops. The chancery's tone is informational. The player writes an introduction.

choices.label: Introduce him as the man who wrote the letter, and say that you are glad he did
choices.outcome: The hall is silent for a second and then applauds, and the applause is the sound the chancery hears on Wednesday when three people call to describe it. The mission is the best-attended in years. {@bishop} says nothing, which is louder. Your name is now attached, publicly, to a position on how bishops conduct themselves, and it will be attached to it for the rest of your life.

choices.label: Introduce him as a preacher and a friend of the pastor, and say nothing of the letter
choices.outcome: It is gracious and it is a page anyone could have written, and the man hears exactly what it leaves out and preaches a magnificent Tuesday anyway. The chancery hears that the vicar was correct. The people who came for the letter are a little disappointed in you and do not say so. You have kept your record clean of a thing you may believe, and he shakes your hand afterward with no reproach at all, which is worse.

choices.label: Introduce him warmly, and say in the same breath that a diocese is governed by its bishop and not by letters
choices.outcome: It is a careful paragraph on ecclesiology and it lands as what it is: a young priest telling a hall full of people that he is not that kind of priest. Half the hall is relieved. The visitor preaches to the other half. The chancery hears about it by Wednesday and writes your name down as sound, and the man, at dinner, says you argued well, and asks whether you believe it, and you tell him.

events.title: The Envelope
events.body: After a funeral at {parish}, a good one, the eldest son of the family finds you in the sacristy while you are still in the alb and puts an envelope in your hand and closes your hand around it and says that this is for you, Father, not for the parish, for you, for what you did for his mother. It is thick. You know without opening it that it is more than a stipend and more than a stole fee and probably more than a month of what the diocese pays you, and he has gone before you can say anything, and the family is in the parking lot, and {@pastor} is at the door of the sacristy in his cassock, watching you hold it. The rule is clear and the practice is not. The stipend goes to the parish. A gift to the priest is the priest's. Where the line is between a gift and a payment for a sacrament is a question canon lawyers have argued and diocesan policies have tried to settle, and the practice in most rectories is that a priest's honesty is the policy. The pastor has seen a great many envelopes. He is looking at you to see what kind of priest was sent to him. Your student loan payment is due on the fifteenth.
events.flavorPrompt: A thick envelope in a sacristy, the pastor watching. The student loan is real. No easy answer.

choices.label: Hand it to the pastor, unopened, for the parish
choices.outcome: He takes it and opens it at the desk and it is two thousand dollars and he whistles. It goes into the collection under the family's name. The son, told by the secretary, is faintly insulted. The pastor says you did not have to, and means it, and something about the way he says it tells you he has, in thirty years, not always. Your loan payment comes out of your salary, as it does.

choices.label: Keep it. He said it was for you, and it was
choices.outcome: The pastor nods once and goes. It is two thousand dollars and it pays the loan for four months and you tell yourself the truth, which is that it was a gift freely given, and the other truth, which is that you would not have been given it if you were not a priest. Nothing is said. The pastor keeps a mental file on vicars and envelopes and you are in it now, and you do not know on which page.

effects.value: Kept a large personal cash gift after a funeral

choices.label: Open it with the pastor, keep the stole fee, and put the rest in the parish under the family's name
choices.outcome: You do the arithmetic aloud, in the sacristy, with the pastor as witness: the diocesan schedule for a funeral, which is yours, and the rest, which is the parish's, receipted to the family for their taxes. The pastor watches you do it and says that is the first time he has seen it done by the book. The son gets a receipt and understands, and is pleased in a way the insult would not have allowed.

events.title: The Book on the Table
events.body: You have left a book on the rectory dinner table, which is a thing you do, and this one is in German. {@pastor} picks it up, looks at the spine, puts it down, and says that the last vicar who read at the table went to the seminary faculty within three years, and that he was a fine teacher and a poor confessor, and that the people of {parish} did not miss him. He says it without malice and he is telling you something. You have heard it elsewhere, in other forms: the usher who said your homily was interesting; the woman at the hospital who asked, kindly, whether you had been a teacher before; the secretary's remark to the DRE that the new Father is very educated. In {parish} it is not a compliment. It is a placement. It means that the parish has decided you are passing through on the way to somewhere with a library, and it will not give you the thing it gives a priest it expects to keep. The pastor pours the wine. He asks whether you have been to see the man on Fourth Street whose wife died in March, and you have not, and he knows you have not, and the book is still on the table.
events.flavorPrompt: A German book on a dinner table. The parish's verdict, delivered kindly, that the vicar is passing through.

choices.label: Go to Fourth Street tomorrow, and keep going, and read in your room
choices.outcome: The man on Fourth Street does not want to talk about his wife and talks about her for two hours. You go back. You go to the others. The book moves upstairs. By Advent the usher has stopped saying interesting and the parish has started, cautiously, to keep you. You have learned that a reputation for learning is a thing a parish forgives only if you are seen to pay for it in visits.

choices.label: Leave the book where it is. You are what you are
choices.outcome: You go to Fourth Street on Thursday and the book stays on the table. The parish's verdict settles. You are the educated one, and you are treated with a respect that has distance in it, and when the chancery looks for a priest to send to a university chaplaincy or a seminary they will find your name already on the pastor's lips. It is not the parish's love. It is a different door.

choices.label: Bring what you know to the parish: a history of {parish} for its centenary, from the archives
choices.outcome: Four months in the diocesan archives and the parish's own basement, and a forty-page booklet with photographs that the parish did not know it had. The families whose grandparents built the church buy it by the box. The educated one has turned out to be useful, which is the only form of learning a parish reliably honors, and the pastor puts a copy in the vestibule and one in his study, and the chancery's newspaper reviews it.

events.title: The Full Nine O'Clock
events.body: The bulletin at {parish} does not say which priest has which Mass, and it never has. But the parish knows, and by your second year the 9:00, which is yours, is full to the doors and has a line at the confessional afterward, and the 10:30, which is {@pastor}'s and was for a decade the parish's Mass, has the empty rows in the back that a pastor sees from the altar and counts. He has not said anything. The secretary has, to the DRE, who has to you, in the form of a joke. The ushers have started putting extra chairs in the side aisle for the 9:00 without being asked. A family that has been at the 10:30 since their wedding has moved to the 9:00 and told the pastor, cheerfully, at the door, that they just love the young priest. He said that he was glad. He said it at dinner too, in a different voice, and then said that a parish should not depend on one man, and he was right, and he was also talking about you. There is a thing you have that he has not had in years and the two of you live in the same house, and he is your pastor, and there is no bulletin listing to hide behind.
events.flavorPrompt: Empty back rows counted from the altar. The pastor's envy is human and not villainous. The vicar has done nothing wrong.

choices.label: Ask him to swap: give him the 9:00 for a season and take the 10:30 yourself
choices.outcome: He says it is not necessary in a voice that says yes. The 9:00 empties a little and the 10:30 fills a little, and the family that loves the young priest follows you to the 10:30, and everyone learns what they already knew. But he sees that you offered, and the presbyterate, which hears about it, decides that you are the kind of vicar who does not build on his pastor's grave. It costs you the line at the confessional for a while.

choices.label: Say nothing and keep preaching. The parish is being fed
choices.outcome: The 9:00 stays full. The chairs stay in the side aisle. You have a following at {parish} that will remember you for twenty years and that will be, when you are moved, the subject of a sentence in your file about a parish that took your transfer hard. The pastor grows shorter with you at dinner and longer in his silences. The presbyterate, which has seen this before, watches to see whether you notice.

choices.label: Preach, at the 9:00, about what the pastor has built here, and mean it
choices.outcome: A homily about the parish, not about him, that is about him in every line: the school kept open, the dying sat with, the roof. The 9:00 hears it and some of them go back to the 10:30 the next week because they have been told, by the young priest they love, whose parish this is. He hears about it from four people before noon. He does not mention it. He pours the wine that night before you sit down.
